youtube_title: Can Marrying Your Witness Keep Them Quiet? 🦝⚖️
caption: Trammel v. United States (1980): in federal court, a spouse can choose to testify against their partner — the privilege belongs to the witness. Private marital communications have a separate protection. Marriage doesn't stop a prosecution.
script: What if you just married the only witness to your crime? [disclaimer] Short answer? Not really. Here's why. This comes from a Supreme Court case from nineteen eighty, Trammel versus United States. A man was charged with smuggling heroin. His wife was in on it too. But she made a deal and agreed to testify against him. He said, you can't do that, she's my wife! Back then, the rule let the accused spouse block that. But the Supreme Court changed it. The Court said the choice belongs to the witness spouse. Nobody can force her to testify against her husband. But nobody can stop her either, if she wants to. So she testified. And he stayed convicted. Ouch! But there's a second, separate rule. Private conversations between married people, the stuff they say just to each other, still get protected. The Court left that rule alone. That's why the trial court kept out the couple's private talks, but still let her say what she saw, and what was said in front of other people. Here's the limit. Marriage doesn't go back in time and protect stuff from before the wedding. It doesn't cover everything a spouse sees. There are exceptions, states have different rules, and getting married never stops a prosecution. [loop] So before you plan a wedding as a legal strategy, remember
